hints: Think about what type of particles exist here, simple covalent $\text{F}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ molecules held together only by weak induced dipole forces.
Compare the size and electron count, iodine has many more electrons than fluorine so its electron cloud is much more easily polarised.
Link stronger van der Waals forces to more energy needed to separate molecules, so decide which substance must have the higher melting point.
walkthrough:
**Identify the forces present**

Both fluorine and iodine exist as simple diatomic molecules, $\text{F}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$. Between molecules there are only van der Waals forces, specifically London dispersion forces.

No hydrogen bonding or permanent dipole-dipole forces here:
$$\text{F}_2 \text{ and } \text{I}_2 \text{ are non-polar} \rightarrow \text{London dispersion forces only}$$

**Compare electron number and polarisability**

Going down Group 17, atoms get bigger with more electrons. Iodine has far more electrons (53 per atom) than fluorine (9 per atom).

More electrons means a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so stronger temporary dipoles form more easily:
$$\text{more electrons} \rightarrow \text{stronger London forces}$$

**Link force strength to melting point**

Stronger intermolecular forces need more thermal energy to break apart when melting. So the substance with stronger forces has the higher melting point.

Therefore $\text{I}_2$ has both stronger van der Waals forces and a higher melting point than $\text{F}_2$:
$$\text{F}_2 < \text{I}_2 \text{ for both melting point and force strength}$$

options.A: Incorrect. This says both melting point and force strength are higher for $\text{F}_2$. In fact $\text{F}_2$ is a gas at room temperature while $\text{I}_2$ is a solid, showing $\text{F}_2$ has weaker forces and a lower melting point.
options.B: Incorrect. Although it correctly states forces are weaker for $\text{F}_2$, it wrongly claims $\text{F}_2$ has the higher melting point. Stronger forces always mean a higher melting point, so the two trends must go in the same direction.
options.C: Correct. $\text{I}_2$ has many more electrons and is more polarisable, so London dispersion forces are stronger between $\text{I}_2$ molecules. More energy is needed to separate them, giving $\text{I}_2$ the higher melting point, so $\text{F}_2 < \text{I}_2$ for both columns.
options.D: Incorrect. It correctly states $\text{F}_2$ has the lower melting point, but wrongly states $\text{F}_2$ has stronger forces. If $\text{F}_2$ really had stronger forces it would need more energy to melt and would have the higher melting point.
